name: Metadata and Ontologies
title: Metadata and Ontologies
answer: Metadata and ontologies cover the structured descriptions that make research data findable, and the formal vocabularies that keep those descriptions consistent across systems. Metadata records what a dataset is, who made it, when, under what licence, and how it relates to other work, while an ontology defines the classes, properties and relationships that those records draw on. In research data and repositories this pairing underpins catalogues, discovery portals and citation, and it is the layer that machine reasoning depends on. The scope runs from lightweight schemas such as Dublin Core through to large domain ontologies used in biomedicine and earth science.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Metadata and ontologies cover the structured descriptions that make research data findable, and the formal vocabularies that keep those descriptions consistent across systems. Metadata records what a dataset is, who made it, when, under what licence, and how it relates to other work, while an ontology defines the classes, properties and relationships that those records draw on. In research data and repositories this pairing underpins catalogues, discovery portals and citation, and it is the layer that machine reasoning depends on. The scope runs from lightweight schemas such as Dublin Core through to large domain ontologies used in biomedicine and earth science.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on repository platforms, metadata schemas and persistent identifier services rather than on model training hardware. Common building blocks include DataCite and Crossref for identifiers and citation records, schema.org and Dublin Core for general description, and domain ontologies published in formats such as RDF, OWL and SKOS. Triple stores and graph databases hold the resulting statements, and APIs such as OAI-PMH and SPARQL expose them to harvesters and search services. Version control and registry services keep vocabularies stable as they change.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Practitioners start from a schema or ontology that fits the domain, then map existing records onto it, often with help from automated extraction over titles, abstracts and full text. Curation follows, where a person checks the mapping, resolves duplicates and confirms that terms mean what the ontology says they mean. Controlled vocabularies and crosswalks between schemas keep records interoperable when they move between repositories. Quality checks look at completeness, consistency and whether identifiers resolve, and the results feed back into the vocabulary as new terms are proposed.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and provenance turn on clear attribution, licence statements and a traceable chain from the dataset back to the work that produced it. Metadata should record the licence, the funder, the contributing institution and any restrictions on reuse, and it should point to the original paper rather than to a secondary summary. Ontology terms carry their own provenance, since a term borrowed from another vocabulary needs its source and version recorded. Privacy and consent obligations apply where records describe people, and community governance decides who may add or deprecate terms.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward machine readable metadata that is rich enough for automated reasoning and for training and evaluation of AI systems. Persistent identifiers, provenance graphs and shared ontologies are converging so that a dataset, its code, its model and its claims can be linked as one object. Large language models are being used to draft metadata and suggest ontology mappings, which shifts human effort toward review rather than creation. The open questions are how to keep vocabularies coherent as they grow and how to credit the curation work that makes any of it usable.
